title: Efficient Human Pose Estimation Leveraging Advanced Techniques with MediaPipe

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper defines elbow angle as the raw difference of two atan2 values: "angle = arctan2(c_y - b_y, c_x - b_x) - arctan2(a_y - b_y, a_x - b_x)" and directly applies thresholds of >160 degrees and <30 degrees. A difference of atan2 values is signed and can range outside the intended unsigned anatomical angle range unless it is wrapped/normalized; for example, equivalent arm configurations can yield negative angles or values near +/-360 degrees. The stated logic therefore does not reliably compute the elbow's interior angle. It should use a normalized absolute angular difference or a dot-product/arccos formulation, normally constrained to [0, 180] degrees.

predicted_errors.error_location: Claims of an "optimized MediaPipe framework" and "refined algorithms" throughout the abstract, methodology, results, and conclusion
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper repeatedly claims "Novel modifications," "comprehensively optimising the underlying algorithms," "refined algorithms," and incorporation of "advanced neural network architectures," but the only concrete pipeline described is standard MediaPipe landmark extraction, pixel-coordinate conversion, a three-landmark angle calculation, and curl-counting thresholds. No modified MediaPipe graph, model architecture, training procedure, loss, optimization, pruning/quantization method, temporal method, or implementation change is specified. An exercise-angle post-processing rule is not a documented optimization of MediaPipe pose estimation itself, so the claimed method cannot be evaluated or reproduced.

The manuscript reports accuracy and speed improvements but gives no evaluable experimental protocol: no dataset names or sizes, number of subjects/samples, train/validation/test partition, ground-truth annotation source, camera specifications, hardware/device, MediaPipe version/configuration, baseline configuration, latency measurement procedure, repetitions, or statistical analysis details. Statements that recordings include walking, running, lighting variation, and natural settings do not establish a reproducible benchmark or a valid comparison.

The system is described as returning normalized body-landmark coordinates, but the paper introduces MSE and IoU without defining the target variables, ground-truth landmarks, coordinate scale, alignment protocol, or the objects for which overlap/union areas are computed. IoU is not defined for a set of point landmarks unless boxes, masks, heatmaps, or a pose-area construction are explicitly specified. Consequently, neither the stated MSE nor IoU constitutes an interpretable pose-accuracy evaluation as presented.

predicted_errors.error_location: Final quantitative-results paragraph: "20% increase" in IoU and "approximately 30%" reduction in processing time
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper asserts a "20% increase in the Intersection over Union (IoU) metric" and a "reduction in processing time by approximately 30%" but provides no baseline value, optimized value, sample size, variation/error bars, device, measurement protocol, statistical test, or underlying table. The claimed quantitative gains therefore cannot be checked and are not supported by reported evidence.

The text says "Table 1 summarizes the experimental data," but no Table 1 or experimental numerical data are present. It also says "Figure 3 demonstrates" real-time multi-keypoint detection, but there is no Figure 3 in the supplied paper; only images labelled Figure 0, Figure 1, and Figure 2 appear. Further, the text identifies Figure 1 as the video-capture/processing architecture and Figure 2 as a processing-time comparison, while the embedded figures are not supplied with corresponding captions or extractable reported values. These missing/misnumbered items make the cited evidence unavailable.

predicted_errors.error_location: MediaPipe description in the introduction and related work
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The manuscript describes MediaPipe as providing "robust, real-time, multi-person pose estimation capabilities" and attributes its on-device pose framework to Google/MediaPipe. The cited BlazePose material concerns MediaPipe's body-pose tracker, whose commonly documented pose solution is primarily a single-person pose tracker; multi-person use requires an explicitly configured multi-pose task/detector setup and is not established by the cited blog. The manuscript neither documents such a setup nor cites support for the blanket multi-person claim.

The bibliography lists: "Cao, Z., Simon, T., Wei, S.E., Sheikh, Y., 2019. Openpose... IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence 32, 172–186." This bibliographic record is incorrect. The TPAMI OpenPose article is associated with IEEE TPAMI volume 43, issue 1, pages 172–186 (published in 2021, with earlier online/preprint versions), not volume 32 in 2019. The citation needs correction.

The cited work "Towards accurate multi-person pose estimation in the wild" is listed as Papandreou et al. (2018), CVPR. This work is a CVPR 2017 paper, not a 2018 CVPR paper, and the author list in the reference is incomplete/misattributed (the paper has additional authors). The year and bibliographic attribution are materially wrong.

predicted_errors.error_location: References "Developer, B., 2020," "Innovator, C., 2021," "Researcher, A., 2021," and "Zhang, Y., et al., 2020"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Several references use placeholder-like author names ("Developer, B.," "Innovator, C.," and "Researcher, A.,") and generic journal titles, and are cited as evidentiary support for central background claims about computational efficiency, sports-analytics robustness, and real-time feedback. These are not adequate verifiable scholarly citations as written and strongly indicate fabricated or unverifiable references. They must be replaced with complete, real, traceable sources or the associated claims removed.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract and conclusion claims that the work "sets a new benchmark" and "substantially advanced the state of the art"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The manuscript claims it "set[s] a new benchmark," has "substantially advanced the state of the art," and is superior to previous literature, yet it reports no named competing methods, no comparable benchmark dataset, no complete numerical results, no standard pose-estimation metric protocol, and no statistical uncertainty. Such state-of-the-art and benchmark conclusions are unsupported by the disclosed methods and results.
